take: The VLCC strike on a Kuwait Oil Tanker Company vessel and the projectile attack at Saudi Arabia's Yanbu port are the dominant crude story, as fresh security risk to Gulf loading infrastructure should steepen the front of the Brent curve even as headline oil dips on Europe tapping diesel reserves. The second theme is the tanker market's structural tightness, with secondhand VLCC values now surpassing newbuild prices — the so-called death zone — whilst MOL's 25-year charter for two 210,000-dwt tri-fuel ore carriers with Vale signals long-haul iron ore demand being locked in and tonne-miles effectively pre-sold. On flows, U.S. crude production is tracking a record 13.8 million b/d in 2026 and propane exports hit 2 million b/d in H1, up 11% year-on-year, so the Atlantic Basin remains long barrels even as Gulf risk premia build. The cross-market link to watch is the diesel complex: Europe drawing down reserves caps gasoil cracks, which in turn softens the incentive to run refineries hard and feeds through to bunker demand, whilst the EIA's $2.93/MMBtu Henry Hub summer average, 6% below last year, keeps LNG-fuelled tonnage economics favourable versus conventional bunkers. For the next 24 hours, watch whether further Hormuz or Yanbu incidents materialise and whether the Baker Hughes rig count decline translates into any downgrade of the 13.8 million b/d forecast, plus any European diesel reserve release data that could extend the crude sell-off.

In 2025, publicly traded companies accounted for just 2% of about 12,000 oil and natural gas producers but produced 68% of the crude oil and natural gas in the Lower 48 states.

items.title: What goes into diesel prices?
items.summary: The price of distillate fuel oil, often sold as diesel, is driven by the price of crude oil, retail margins, distribution costs, taxes, and crack spreads, the indicator we use for refining margins. Tight global supplies of distillate fuel oil and elevated crude oil prices have driven prices higher in recent months.
